Baltimore's four Trash Wheels sit at the mouths of streams and rivers and
lift floating rubbish out of the water before it reaches the harbour. Every
full dumpster is recorded, along with estimated counts of seven kinds of
rubbish.

This package is for **Healthy Harbor volunteers and community educators**
who want to answer one question:

> Which kinds of rubbish does each Trash Wheel collect most, and is it going
> up or down over time?

This guide shows how to install the package, use the app, read its results,
and do the same analysis in your own R code.

## 1. Install the package

Install the package from GitHub with the `remotes` package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-prat0012-ai")
```

Then load it:

```{r}
library(trashwheels)
```

## 2. Launch the app

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
```

The app opens in your web browser. It uses the data inside the package, so
it needs no other files or internet connection.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "The Trash Wheel rubbish explorer app, with four numbered controls on the left and a line chart of plastic bottles per dumpster load on the right."}
knitr::include_graphics("app-overview.png")
```

## 3. Use the controls

The controls on the left are numbered in the order you would normally use
them.

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| 1. Choose a kind of rubbish | Picks one of the seven kinds of rubbish, for example plastic bottles or cigarette butts. Everything on the page then describes only this kind. |
| 2. Choose the Trash Wheels to compare | Each ticked Trash Wheel gets its own line. They started at different times: Mister in 2014, Professor in 2017, Captain in 2018 and Gwynnda in 2021. |
| 3. Choose the years | Drag either end of the slider to narrow the period. |
| 4. Choose what to measure | **Average items per dumpster load** is the fair comparison. **Total items per year** shows how much was collected in total. |

The page has three tabs. **Trend over time** shows the chart, **Yearly
numbers** shows the exact figures behind it, and **About the data** explains
every field and where the data come from.

## 4. Read the results

The headline above the chart states the main result for your current
choices. It names the Trash Wheel with the highest value and gives the
number. The sentence below it explains how to read the chart and whether the
leading Trash Wheel's numbers rose or fell over the chosen years.

In the chart, each line is one Trash Wheel and its name sits at the end of
the line. A higher line means more of that rubbish. A falling line means less
of it over time.

Solid points are based on 5 or more counted dumpster loads. Hollow points
are based on fewer than 5, so one unusual load can move them a lot. Treat
them with care.

The orange **Read with care** box lists anything in your selection that
could mislead, such as a Trash Wheel that did not count the chosen item, or
a year where the item was counted in only some of the loads.

### Why the average per load matters

The number of dumpsters filled changes a lot from year to year and from
wheel to wheel. Mister Trash Wheel filled 44 dumpsters in 2014 but 93 in
2018. A bigger total can simply mean more dumpsters, not dirtier water.

Wrappers show this clearly. Mister Trash Wheel collected the most wrappers
in total, but Professor Trash Wheel collected the most in each dumpster load:

```{r}
wrappers <- summarise_rubbish(trash_loads, item = "Wrappers")

# Highest total: Mister Trash Wheel
totals <- tapply(wrappers$total_items, wrappers$wheel, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
round(totals)

# Highest average per load: Professor Trash Wheel
loads_counted <- tapply(wrappers$loads_counted, wrappers$wheel, sum)
round(totals / loads_counted)
```

This is why the app starts with the average per load.

### When there is nothing fair to show

Some Trash Wheels never counted some kinds of rubbish. For example, Gwynnda
Trash Wheel never counted glass bottles. A blank record means "not counted",
not zero, so the app does not draw a misleading line at zero. It explains
what is missing and suggests what to try instead.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "The app showing an orange message that glass bottles were not counted by Gwynnda Trash Wheel, with a suggestion to try another kind of rubbish."}
knitr::include_graphics("app-not-counted.png")
```

## 5. Do the same analysis in R

The app is built from two functions that you can use yourself.

`summarise_rubbish()` gives one row per Trash Wheel and year:

```{r}
bottles <- summarise_rubbish(
  trash_loads,
  item = "Plastic bottles",
  years = c(2019, 2023)
)
bottles
```

`plot_rubbish()` draws the same chart as the app:

```{r, fig.alt = "Line chart of average plastic bottles per dumpster load from 2019 to 2023. Professor Trash Wheel is highest but falling, from about 5,750 to 3,800 per load."}
plot_rubbish(bottles, measure = "per_load")
```

From 2019 to 2023, Professor Trash Wheel collected the most plastic bottles
in each load, but its average fell from about 5,750 to about 3,800 per load.
The other three Trash Wheels stayed between about 1,100 and 2,200 per load.

## 6. Limits to keep in mind

* **Counts are estimates.** The Trash Wheel team counts a sample of each
  dumpster and scales it up.
* **The data show what was collected, not why.** A fall could come from less
  litter, less rain washing rubbish into the streams, or changes in how the
  counts were made.
* **Not every item was counted everywhere.** Check the Yearly numbers tab
  before comparing Trash Wheels.

## Data source

Mr. Trash Wheel, part of Baltimore's Healthy Harbor initiative
(<https://www.mrtrashwheel.com/>), shared through TidyTuesday on 5 March 2024.
The script `data-raw/trash_loads.R` in the GitHub repository shows every
cleaning step.
